title: Fractional CFO vs CPA: What Each One Owns
summary: Fractional CFO vs CPA comes down to who looks forward and who closes the year. See what each one owns and which one your business needs first.
body_markdown:
## Fractional CFO vs CPA: Where the Work Divides


Fractional CFO vs CPA comes down to two things, the direction the work faces and what the work produces. You know the March call. Your accountant walks you through a year that’s already finished, every figure correct, and nobody in the conversation mentions the next one. That gap isn’t a service failure. At indinero we read it as two different jobs looking at the same ledger, and most established businesses end up needing both.


**The direction the work faces.** A CPA engagement is anchored to a period that’s over. The ledger is closed, the numbers are final, and the job is to characterize them correctly for someone outside the business. A fractional CFO engagement is anchored to a period that hasn’t happened yet. The numbers are assumptions, they will be wrong in detail, and the job is to narrow the range enough that you can decide with it.


Same ledger. Opposite ends of the calendar.


**What the work produces.** This is the sharper cut, and most comparisons miss it. CPA work produces an artifact for an external reader who holds authority over you. A filed return. A reviewed or audited financial statement. A written position that holds up in an examination. CFO work produces an internal decision, a plan, or a reallocation of money. A rolling forecast. A margin schedule that reprices a service line. A model that says lease, not buy.


The audience is the real divide. One set of numbers is written to satisfy a reader who can penalize you. The other is written to be acted on by the people who run the company.


**Who holds the authority.** The[IRS](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/understanding-tax-return-preparer-credentials-and-qualifications) is explicit that only enrolled agents, certified public accountants, and attorneys hold unlimited representation rights, meaning they can represent a client on any matter including audits, collection issues, and appeals. That standing comes from a license, not from operating experience. A CFO’s authority runs the other direction, inside the business, over how money gets planned and spent. Neither one substitutes for the other.


Framed as CFO vs accountant, the comparison sounds like a contest. It isn’t. The[Journal of Accountancy](https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2023/mar/the-changing-role-of-the-cfo/) describes finance leadership shifting away from preparing information on historic results and policing spending limits, toward supplying forward-looking insight, with one CFO in that account describing the job as anticipating what will happen and how the business will react under various scenarios. Backward-looking accuracy didn’t become less important. It stopped being the whole job. If what you actually want is the[internal finance role ladder](https://www.indinero.com/blog/controller-vs-comptroller-vs-cfo/) , that comparison is covered separately, and this page stays on the two-role question it promised.


## What Your CPA Owns and Why It Stays There


Your CPA owns work governed by enforceable professional standards, bound to statutory deadlines, and in some cases restricted by license. A fractional CFO doesn’t take that over. Nobody should want them to.


The AICPA reorganized its enforceable tax practice standards effective January 1, 2024, and the structure of that revision is a clean map of what sits on the CPA side of the line.


- **General standards.** SSTS No. 1 applies to all tax services, covering advice on tax positions, knowledge of errors, data protection, and reliance on tools.
- **Tax compliance.** SSTS No. 2 governs tax return positions, tax return questions, reliance on information from others, use of estimates, and departure from previous positions.
- **Tax consulting.** SSTS No. 3 governs advisory work on a specific issue, separate from the preparation of the return itself.
- **Representation.** SSTS No. 4, new in the revision, governs representing clients before tax authorities in examinations and appeals ([The Tax Adviser](https://www.thetaxadviser.com/issues/2023/nov/understanding-the-updated-tax-ethical-standards/) ).


Attestation and assurance sit here too. Audits, reviews, and compilations. A lender, bonding agent, franchisor, or acquirer who wants third-party assurance on your statements is asking for something only a licensed firm can give them. So do entity and multi-state filing obligations, information returns, and the year-end package itself.


All of it is built on a closed period. That’s the common thread.


Here’s the piece most comparisons never mention, and it’s the strongest argument in this section. If any part of your CPA firm’s work for you is attest work, that firm is constrained by rule in how much management thinking it can do for you. The AICPA Code of Professional Conduct’s general requirements for performing nonattest services, at ET section 1.295.040, say the CPA cannot assume management’s responsibilities, and the firm has to be satisfied before the engagement begins that the client is both willing and able to perform all management functions related to it. You agree to assume management responsibilities, designate an individual with suitable skills and experience to oversee the service, evaluate the adequacy and results of the work, and accept responsibility for the results. A practitioner quoted in the[Journal of Accountancy](https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2016/nov/maintaining-independence-with-nonattest-services/) puts the boundary plainly for smaller clients: “we can either do your bookkeeping or your audit, but not both.”


Read that from the owner’s chair. The rules that protect the integrity of your attest relationship actively push management decisions back onto your side of the table, and your CPA isn’t permitted to close that gap for you. That isn’t a criticism of your accountant. It’s a structural reason to put forward-looking financial leadership on your own side.


Which raises the obvious follow-up: does a fractional CFO have to be a CPA? No. The license is evidence of technical depth on a closed period, not evidence of forecasting judgment, pricing discipline, or experience running a finance function at your level of complexity. Plenty of capable fractional CFOs hold it. Plenty don’t. And if what you need right now is a return prepared or a notice answered, that work belongs to[indinero’s business tax team](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) , not to a CFO engagement.


## What a Fractional CFO Adds to the Same Numbers


A fractional CFO doesn’t produce a new set of books. It changes who the numbers are written for, and it adds four kinds of work a closed period can’t do.


- **See Clearly.** Profitability by product, service, customer, and segment, down to the underlying unit economics. A tight set of leading and lagging indicators on a dashboard leadership can steer by. Management reporting written as a narrative about what’s coming, not a restatement of what happened.
- **Plan Forward.** Rolling forecasts of revenue, expense, profit, and cash impact, updated as conditions change rather than set once a year. Cash flow and working capital management. Scenario planning for hiring phases, new locations, and capital investment. This theme runs on a cadence and never finishes.
- **Decide Well.** One pending decision at a time, modeled before you commit. Lease versus buy on a building or a piece of equipment. The fully costed margin on a large contract before it’s signed. Whether a second location pays for itself, and on what timeline. Whether to raise prices, on which lines, and how much volume the margin can absorb. Where to deploy accumulated cash instead of letting it sit.
- **Build Value.** Process improvement across the close, billing, and collections. Working Capital Optimization as an active lever on trapped cash. Finance function and team design. Building enterprise value over years, so the business is worth more and runs well without you in it.


Here’s the visibility gap in plain terms. A tax return tells you the business made money last year. It can’t tell you that a handful of customers consume a disproportionate share of delivery hours, or that your second-largest service line carries your thinnest margin. That answer requires assigning revenue and cost to each customer or segment instead of reporting them in total. Segment revenue minus segment cost gives segment profitability, and dividing that by segment revenue gives the margin percentage. The arithmetic is unglamorous, and peer-reviewed work in PLOS ONE on customer profitability analysis finds its value sits in decision-making rather than in reporting. The data is usually already sitting in your general ledger.


Nobody has been asked to cut it that way.


The planning gap has a number attached to it. The Association for Financial Professionals defines the[cash conversion cycle](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/glossary/cash-conversion-cycle) as a measurement of the time a company must finance the costs of making products or delivering services before receiving payment for them, calculated as days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding minus days payable outstanding. Translate that for the owner who says the profit is there but the bank balance never is. If you deliver the work in May, invoice in June, and collect in August while payroll and suppliers are paid in May, the business is lending money to its customers for three months and funding that loan from somewhere.


Growth makes it worse, not better.


Not just more reporting, then, but reporting built to be acted on. That’s the work[indinero CFO Services](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) are scoped around, and the[guide to CFO service models](https://www.indinero.com/blog/the-complete-guide-to-cfo-service-models/) covers how the engagement itself gets structured.


## Which One Your Business Needs First


Compliance first, clean books second, strategic leadership third. That order isn’t about importance. It’s about dependency.


Filings carry statutory deadlines with penalties attached, so they aren’t optional and they don’t wait. There’s no forecast worth building on top of an unfiled return.


Then the close. A forecast inherits the quality of the history underneath it. If revenue is recognized inconsistently, if the bank hasn’t been reconciled in four months, or if cost of delivery is mixed into general overhead, a segment margin analysis will produce a confident answer that happens to be wrong. That’s worse than no answer, because you’ll act on it.


Then the strategic layer, which is where the fractional CFO belongs and where the value compounds. Every month of dependable history makes the next forecast better.


**Readiness is complexity, not size.** There’s no revenue number at which a business becomes CFO-ready, and funding stage is beside the point. What creates the need is operational complexity. More products, more locations, more customer types, more suppliers, and decisions larger than any you’ve made before. The question owners actually type is “do I need a CFO or a CPA,” and the honest answer depends on which of these sentences you’ve said out loud lately.


- Profitable on paper, but there’s never enough cash.
- Growth feels more chaotic, not less.
- Margins are slipping and I can’t tell you why.
- We’re sitting on cash with no plan for it.
- There’s a decision in front of me bigger than anything I’ve decided before.


For the longer read on timing, see[when to hire a CFO](https://www.indinero.com/blog/when-to-hire-a-cfo-stage-guide/) . The faster route is to start from what you’re actually feeling rather than from a job title.


What you’re actually feeling Where it goes first


A return is due, a notice arrived, or a lender wants the year-end package Tax and compliance


The books are behind, or I don’t trust the monthly numbers Accounting and the close, then CFO


I can’t tell which products, services, or customers make money CFO, See Clearly


Profitable but cash is always tight, and growth makes it worse CFO, Plan Forward


One large decision is pending and I need it modeled before I commit CFO, Decide Well


I want the business worth more and running without me in it CFO, Build Value


Most established, growing businesses end up with both roles and a boundary everyone involved can state out loud. This isn’t an argument for replacing your accountant. The question was never whether your accountant is good. It’s whether anyone’s job is the next twelve months.


A preparer’s job ends when the return is accepted.


If the real problem is the books,[indinero accounting services](https://www.indinero.com/services/accounting-services/) handle the cleanup and the monthly close, and the difference between[bookkeeping and accounting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/bookkeeping-vs-accounting/) sorts out which of the two you’re missing.


## How Indinero Runs CFO Work Alongside Tax and Compliance


At indinero, accounting, tax, and CFO work sit under one roof and stay in their lanes. Coordinated, not merged.


Accounting produces the numbers. The close, the reconciliations, the monthly financial statements. Tax prepares and files, including information returns and representation when a notice arrives. CFO uses the numbers, building the forecast, the margin and working capital analysis, the decision models, and the management reporting set leadership steers by.


The line holds in both directions. The CFO designs the reporting roadmap and tells the accounting team what management reporting has to show. The accounting team builds it. The CFO reads it and decides with it. The CFO does not produce the close, and the CFO does not prepare or sign a return.


**What CFO and CPA working together looks like across a year.** Not a promise. A rhythm.


- The CFO hands the forecast to tax, so estimated payments reflect where the year is heading instead of what last year happened to be.
- Tax sends back the treatment and the cash consequence, and the CFO puts that consequence into the forecast as a real outflow on a real date.
- Decisions with tax consequences get flagged before they happen rather than discovered in the spring. Timing of a capital purchase. Lease versus buy. Activity starting in a new state. A change in owner compensation.
- The year-end package gets assembled from a close that already exists, with the support schedules the preparer asked for, instead of being reconstructed under deadline.
- The tax position itself stays the tax team’s judgment and the tax team’s signature. The CFO doesn’t make that call.


**If you’re keeping the CPA you already have.** Plenty of owners have a twenty-year accountant relationship they aren’t going to end, and they shouldn’t have to. CFO work is built to hand off cleanly to an outside preparer. A consistent chart of accounts, a close that lands on a schedule, and documentation that answers questions before they’re asked. Your accountant’s year-end gets easier, not harder. And given the independence requirements described above, having capable management thinking on your side of the table is exactly what those rules assume you already have.


Indinero has maintained continuous operations since 2009 and works with 500+ regular customers. Engagements are scoped to the complexity of the financial leadership a business actually needs, which is why the CFO conversation starts with your decisions rather than with a package.

If you need the books fixed first, that’s accounting. If you need a return prepared, that’s[business tax](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) . ## Frequently asked questions


Owners weighing a fractional CFO against the accountant they already pay tend to arrive with the same short list of questions. The answers below cover the credential question, what a CFO can and can’t do on a tax return, where to start when the books are behind, and what to ask before you sign anything.


### Does a fractional CFO have to be a CPA?


No, a fractional CFO doesn’t have to hold a CPA license, because that credential certifies technical depth on a closed period, not forecasting judgment. A CPA license comes from a state board through education, a uniform exam, and supervised experience, all of it earned on historical reporting, audit, and tax. Many capable fractional CFOs hold it and many don’t. Indinero scopes CFO engagements to the decisions a business is facing, so ask about forecasting, pricing, and margin by customer instead.


### Can a fractional CFO prepare and file our business tax return?


No, a fractional CFO doesn’t prepare or file business tax returns, and at indinero that work sits with the business tax team instead. The IRS requires anyone paid to prepare a federal return to hold a preparer tax identification number, and unlimited representation rights belong to CPAs, enrolled agents, and attorneys. Return preparation also has its own enforceable standard under the revised AICPA tax standards. A CFO coordinates on planning and flags decisions with tax consequences, then the tax team signs.


### Will a fractional CFO replace the CPA firm we already use?


No, a fractional CFO doesn’t replace your CPA firm, and most established businesses keep both roles with a clear boundary between them. There’s a rule-based reason to keep your accountant and add leadership on your own side. Under the AICPA nonattest services requirements at ET section 1.295.040, a firm doing attest work for you can’t assume management’s responsibilities, and you have to designate someone with suitable skills to oversee the work. A fractional CFO is who holds that chair.


### If our books are behind, do we start with a CPA or a CFO?


Start with the close, not the CFO, because unreconciled books produce a confident forecast that happens to be wrong. Statutory filing deadlines don’t wait, so current returns come first, and a monthly close that lands on a schedule comes next. That cleanup and the ongoing close sit with indinero accounting services. CFO work becomes useful as soon as the close is dependable, which doesn’t take years of clean history.


### How do a CFO and a tax preparer coordinate during the year?


The CFO works the open period and the tax preparer works the closed one, with the forecast as the handoff between them. The CFO supplies a current forecast so estimated payments reflect where the year is heading. The tax preparer sends back the treatment and the cash consequence, and the CFO puts that outflow in the forecast on a dated line. Large purchase timing, a new state, and owner compensation structure get flagged before the decision rather than discovered in the spring.


### What should we ask a fractional CFO about working with our accountant?


Ask who owns the monthly close, what date it lands, and exactly what the CFO will need from your accountant and when. Ask whether they’ll contact your accountant directly or route everything through you, whether they’ll change your chart of accounts or close checklist, and which decisions they’ll flag for tax review before you make them. Ask what they don’t do. And ask what you keep if the engagement ends, which models and which schedules.
